options.text: The period doubles to $0.889\text{ s}$, because the block has twice as far to travel.
options.why: Thinks a longer path means a longer period, ignoring that the speed also increases.

options.text: The period stays $0.444\text{ s}$ and the maximum speed doubles to $1.41\text{ m/s}$, because $T=2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$ does not depend on the amplitude while $v_{max}=A\sqrt{k/m}$ does.
options.why: The period depends only on the mass and the spring constant, and the maximum speed is proportional to the amplitude.

options.text: The period stays $0.444\text{ s}$ and the maximum speed stays $0.707\text{ m/s}$, because both depend only on the mass and the spring constant.
options.why: Applies the amplitude independence of the period to the maximum speed as well.

options.text: The period halves to $0.222\text{ s}$, because a larger amplitude means a larger restoring force.
options.why: Thinks a larger restoring force shortens the period, forgetting that the distance traveled increases too.

options.text: The speed is greatest at the equilibrium position because the net force is largest there.
options.why: Thinks the net force is largest at the equilibrium position, where it is actually zero.

options.text: The speed is greatest at the endpoints of the motion, because the spring force is largest there.
options.why: Mixes up the largest force with the largest speed; the block is momentarily at rest at the endpoints.

options.text: The speed is the same everywhere, $0.5\text{ m/s}$, because the total mechanical energy is constant.
options.why: Confuses a constant total energy with a constant speed; the energy changes form.

options.text: The speed is greatest at the equilibrium position, $0.5\text{ m/s}$, because all of the energy is kinetic there and the spring's elastic energy is zero.
options.why: Energy conservation gives $\tfrac12kA^2=\tfrac12mv_{max}^2$ at the equilibrium position.

ap_physics_1-m28.stem: A student measures the period of a simple pendulum for several string lengths using small amplitudes. The table shows the data. Which of the following is best supported by the data?

stimulus.description: Length and period of a pendulum

options.text: The product $TL$ is nearly constant, so longer pendulums have shorter periods.
options.why: Reads a decreasing quantity as an inverse relationship, but the period increases with the length in the table.

options.text: When the length increases from $0.20\text{ m}$ to $0.80\text{ m}$, the period increases by the same factor of $4$.

options.why: Tests the ratio $T/L$ for a direct proportion, but for these data it falls from $4.51$ to $2.24$ s/m.

options.text: The quantity $T^2/L$ is nearly constant, about $4.07\text{ s}^2\text{/m}$, so the data support $T$ proportional to $\sqrt{L}$.
options.why: The values of $T^2/L$ range only from $4$ to $4.12$ s^2/m, which is consistent with $T=2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$.

ap_physics_1-m29.stem: A solid block floats at rest in water with part of its volume below the surface. The same block is placed in a liquid with $3$ times the density of water and floats at rest again. By what factor does the volume of the block below the surface change?

Thinks the submerged volume is the same because the buoyant force equals the same weight, forgetting that the displaced volume depends on the density.

stimulus.description: Position of an object along a line

options.why: Confuses an increasing displacement with an increasing acceleration; a constant acceleration makes the displacement increase by the same amount each interval.

options.text: The displacement in each successive 1.0 s interval (2 m, 4 m, 6 m, 8 m) increases by the same $2\text{ m}$, so the object has a constant acceleration of $2\text{ m/s}^2$.

options.text: The acceleration is $2.75\text{ m/s}^2$, because $a=2x/t^2$ for the position 22 m at 4.0 s.
options.why: Uses the constant-acceleration relation $x=\tfrac12at^2$ as if the object had started at the origin from rest, ignoring the initial position and velocity in the data.

options.text: The object moves $2\text{ m}$ or more in every second, so its velocity is constant.
options.why: Reads a position that keeps increasing as a constant velocity, although the displacement in each interval is different.
